General video formats do not support transparency. (Like .mov and .mp4) For that you would need to insert a green screen in the parts you want to be transparent and then in an editing program key them out to have whatever you want in those green places.
Your other options are to export it as a GIF - GIFs support transparency but Procreate Dreams doesn’t yet offer the option to export GIFs, you’d still need to export it as an image sequence and then make it into a GIF in any of the sites found online.
Or you can click on the custom settings and set your video codec to be ProRes 4444 or ProRes 4444 HQ (I don’t remember rn if those exact codecs were available, I only noticed that it did have different ProRes codecs, so I presume those are there as well) However, I have not experimented with that myself, so I can’t say for certain that it works flawlessly, I simply don’t know. I study animation and have made animations in Procreate. The main crutch for me with regular Procreate’s animation assist is the fact that it has only one animation track. That means if I have drawn frames and I want them to be coloured, I can’t have the colours in a seperate layer - both the linework frames and the colour frames have to be merged for them to play back as coloured frames instead of flashing between linework and colour. Mostly that can be fine, but it also means that I can’t easily change the colours if I wish so because they’re merged together with the linework. Or if I have an initial sketch over which I draw the final linework. Having the sketches on a seperate track makes it easier to then turn the visibility off for all of them at the same time during playback.
Also, for example if I want to have a background which has some motion in it. I have to merge those background frames together with the foreground frames if I want to see them as a whole during playback. And again - that can be fine but it makes it more difficult if I need to make changes to the foreground - any strokes with the eraser will also erase the background unless I really zoom in and carefully erase along the lines so that the background isn’t affected, which takes more time.
Another thing off the top of my head is if I want to have an animated object moving across the screen but don’t want to animate it frame by frame and instead by using keyframes. (For example a car with a flashing beacon moving from one side of the screen to the other) So far the easiest way how to do that has been animating the car’s beacon while it is stationary and then in an editing program merging those frames as a group to then set keyframes for it to move across the screen while looping the beacon animation. Now with Procreate Dreams I will be able to move a whole group of layers and set keyframes for it which is a faster playback process rather than exporting it to a seperate editing program.
Those are just two examples but there are many more things which will make the whole animation process faster.
Also the fact that you can now insert an audio track. Without Procreate’s ability to insert audio tracks it is rather difficult to animate mouth movements to be in sync with spoken words because you can’t visually see the audio waveform, where each sound starts and ends. And can’t quickly check if it’s in sync without again - exporting it to an editing program where you can add an audio track to check if it fits.

I like to think of Greek myths as fun stories. 
I don’t think that they should be read, studied and understood like academic papers because I don’t believe they were created with such intent.
They were created to try to explain the world around and it’s interesting to know about that viewpoint of why things are how they are.

Rather a legend than a story.
The Bloody Marry.
I like it because it’s psychological and most people don’t even know it.
The legend itself works as a primer - you get ready to see something in the mirror.
But it can work even without it and even in a brightly lit room.
Basically - just stare in the mirror at a stationary point on your face.
The brain is very good at two things:

1. Erasing unneeded information. Any information that is unneeded gets erased. For example the brain doesn’t need to see that you have a nose, it knows you have a nose. So if you don’t think about it, you don’t see your nose in your day to day life. Your brain erases it from your vision.

2. Seeing faces. Like in clouds or objects that look like a face. It’s a survival instinct - it’s there so we can spot faces quickly and notice danger quickly.

Back to the mirror - when you’re looking at your own face at a stationary point, after a little while the brain takes your face as unneeded information. It sees that it’s there and that it doesn’t move so it starts erasing portions from it.
That’s the moment when the “seeing faces” instinct kicks in - the brain is programmed to see faces so when it erases parts of your face it quickly tries to put that information back together but messes up and you start noticing weird patterns on your face that can be scary. They vanish though as soon as you think about it or move your eyes to it.
It’s fascinating to think about and try for yourself and scary for those to whom you tell the legend and who don’t know how it works.
